title: Working Within Authorization and Escalation Boundaries

content.overview: Competent technicians know both what they are trained to do and where their authority ends. This lesson teaches routine action, stop-work and escalation boundaries.

vocabulary.definition: Formal permission based on role, training, procedure or assignment to perform a defined action.
Under OSHA lockout/tagout terminology, an employee who operates or uses equipment being serviced or works where covered servicing occurs.
Under OSHA lockout/tagout terminology, an employee authorized to apply energy-control devices for covered servicing or maintenance.

sections.title: Capability is not authorization
sections.body: Recognizing a pesticide restriction, electrical problem, equipment fault or biosecurity hold does not give a technician authority to clear it. Technician I is a routine operational credential, not unrestricted technical authority.

sections.title: Know the maintenance boundary
sections.body: OSHA hazardous-energy rules distinguish affected from authorized employees for covered servicing. When work requires protected access, defeating a guard, opening energized equipment or servicing beyond the assigned operator procedure, the Technician I response is to stop and refer the condition.

workedExamples: A pump alarm may permit a defined external operator check but not opening an electrical panel.
A held room remains restricted until the authorized role clears the hold under procedure.
commonMistakes: Bypassing a guard or control to finish faster.
content.practicalApplication: Classify twelve actions as routine-authorized, stop/hold, maintenance referral, supervisor decision, safety response or emergency response using supplied role rules.
content.summary: Professional performance includes stopping at the correct boundary. Technicians complete authorized routine work and escalate regulated, hazardous, maintenance or supervisory decisions.
